Kioniskos of Malthake of Hagnous

IG II2 5271 Date: 2nd century BC
 
Malthake daughter of - of Hagnous, wife of Theoxenos of -.[1] relief
Previous - IG II2 5261 Next - IG II2 5374
References:
IG II2 5271 (Translated text) (PHI)
Translation by: Emma Buhrman
Monument type: Kioniskos
Inscription type: Funerary
Findspot: Unknown (EM 11614)
Transliterations on Places on
[1] This funerary kioniskos (small column) commemorates Malthake, an Athenian citizen who is identified as a priestess by the relief depiction of an angular temple key, a common symbol for priestesses on Classical and Hellenistic Attic funerary monuments. Priesthoods are one of very few professions we find explicitly acknowledged on Athenian gravestones in sculpture or inscriptions (see AIUK 4.6 (BM funerary), no. 23 for the priestess Choirine; J. B. Connelly, Portrait of a Priestess, 2007, ch. 8). Relief decoration on these gravestones tends to associate priests with sacrificial knives and priestesses with keys. For other funerary monuments for priestesses, see IG I3 1330; IG II2 6232, 6288, 6398, 6945, 7244, 7356, 11392, 12200, 12292, SEG 22.199. There is a particular reluctance among citizens to designate themselves by their jobs, but roles such as priestesses and soldiers were perhaps appropriate to display to the passersby since they indicate the performance of citizen duties (on occupational terms in dedications, see IG I3 546, with notes). Monuments for non-citizens also rarely refer to the deceased’s profession, but we find a number of categories of household servants and slaves, such as wet-nurses (see AIUK 4.6 (BM funerary), no. 37) and paidagogoi (who supervised young boys, e.g. IG II2 6397). On kioniskoi, see AIUK 3 (Fitzwilliam), no. 7 with notes.
